title: Voltage Divider: Why Two Resistors Split the Voltage
topic: Voltage divider — two resistors in series across a source put V_out = V_in · R2/(R1+R2) at the midpoint; sweeping R2 sweeps V_out proportionally

beats.narration: Two resistors stacked across a voltage source — what voltage shows up between them?

elements.content: Manimo bobs in centre-screen
Two resistors, one input — where does V out land?

beats.narration: Send V in across R one and R two in series — Kirchhoff says the two drops have to add up to V in.

elements.content: Battery on left with + and − terminal lines
Top wire from battery + to top of R1, bottom wire from R2 bottom back to battery −
R1 zigzag (upper resistor)
R2 zigzag (lower resistor)
V_in label on the battery
R1 and R2 labels next to each resistor
V_out probe tapping the midpoint between R1 and R2
Charge dots travelling clockwise around the loop — the same current through R1 and R2
the same current threads both resistors

beats.narration: The same current flows through both, so V out equals V in times R two divided by R one plus R two.

elements.content: V_in = V_R1 + V_R2
I = V_in / (R1 + R2)
V_out = I · R2
V_out = V_in · R2/(R1+R2)
V out is V in scaled by R2's share of the total

beats.narration: Scrub R two. As it grows from small to large, V out climbs from near zero up toward V in — proportionally.

beats.narration: The output is V in scaled by R two's share of the total resistance — that's the voltage divider.

elements.content: V_out = V_in · R2 / (R1 + R2)
R1 = R2 → half. R2 ≫ R1 → almost V_in. R2 ≪ R1 → almost zero.
